recommendations.action: For microwave links, check received signal level and modulation changes; for fibre, check optical power levels

recommendations.rationale: Identify configuration or path changes that may have introduced congestion or mis‑prioritization

answer.summary: Five similar cases were identified, all showing high alarm counts together with degraded cell availability and signal strength. The dominant pattern points to alarm storms triggered by equipment faults, transport QoS issues, or radio coverage problems, leading to poor service quality across multiple cells.

likely_causes.cause: Failing hardware (radio units, power modules, fans, transceivers)
Software defects or memory leaks causing repeated restarts
Over-temperature from cooling failures
Upstream fault (transport or power) raising secondary alarms (alarm storm)
Previous repairs that treated symptoms only, leading to recurring faults

recommendations.action: Group active alarms by type and site to isolate the root alarm from secondary alarms.
recommendations.rationale: Alarm storms usually start from a single root event; grouping helps focus troubleshooting.

recommendations.action: Suppress duplicate secondary alarms and focus on the root alarm.
recommendations.rationale: Reduces noise and enables corrective action on the underlying cause.

recommendations.action: Check hardware health (temperatures, fan status, power-supply readings) at affected sites.
recommendations.rationale: Over-temperature or power issues are common root causes of alarm storms.

recommendations.action: If the alarm indicates a software hang, restart the affected software process or unit (requires change approval).
recommendations.rationale: Software defects or memory leaks can cause repeated restarts and alarms.

recommendations.action: Dispatch field operations for critical hardware alarms at busy sites to replace faulty hardware or repair cooling systems.
recommendations.rationale: Failing hardware or cooling failures drive alarm storms and degraded KPIs.
